body:
Meaning and purpose of the Sangha

As the Buddha's teachings spread, people began leaving household life to follow his path of discipline, meditation and learning. The Buddha established an organised community of such followers, known as the Buddhist Sangha.

The Sangha was the organised Buddhist monastic community whose members renounced ordinary household life, followed rules of conduct and worked towards spiritual liberation.

Members of the monastic community studied and practised the Buddha's teachings, known as Dhamma in Pali or Dharma in Sanskrit. They also taught these principles to other people.

The Sangha gave Buddhism an organised institution through which teachings could be preserved, practised and transmitted from one generation to another.

Monks, nuns and lay followers

The Buddhist community included ordained religious members and lay supporters. These groups played different but connected roles.

  • Bhikkhus: Ordained Buddhist monks who had renounced household life. The word refers to those who live on alms.
  • Bhikkhunis: Ordained Buddhist nuns who followed a disciplined religious life within the women's monastic community.
  • Lay followers: Men and women who accepted Buddhist teachings while continuing ordinary household life. They supported the monks and nuns through donations and other assistance.

Monks and nuns formed the ordained Sangha. Lay supporters were important to the wider Buddhist community but did not become monks or nuns merely by accepting the Buddha's teachings.

Membership and social background

The Buddha's followers came from different sections of society. The Sangha included people who had previously been kings, merchants, craftspeople, labourers and enslaved persons. People from different social backgrounds could enter the monastic order rather than membership being reserved for a single hereditary group.

According to the Buddhist ideal described in early texts, members left their former social identities behind on entering the monastic community. Their conduct and religious discipline became more important than distinctions based on birth.

Admission nevertheless involved rules and restrictions. Children needed parental permission. Early accounts also describe permission requirements: enslaved persons needed their masters' permission, debtors their creditors' permission and people serving the king the king's permission. These conditions reflected the social and legal relationships within which the early Sangha operated.

Daily life and monastic discipline

Members of the Sangha were expected to lead simple lives. They possessed few personal belongings, practised meditation, studied the Dhamma and taught others.

Bhikkhus commonly visited villages and towns to receive food as alms. They depended on householders for food and other necessities rather than maintaining ordinary household occupations.

Monastic discipline also governed the handling of possessions, food, accommodation and relationships within the community. The collection of these regulations became part of the Vinaya Pitaka.

The rainy-season retreat and monasteries

Early Buddhist monks travelled from place to place to teach. During the rainy season, travelling became difficult, so they remained in one place for a period of retreat. This practice is known as Vassa.

Initially, monks used temporary shelters, gardens and natural caves. Over time, permanent monasteries called viharas developed. Kings, wealthy merchants and other supporters donated land, buildings and necessities for monastic life.

How the Sangha made decisions

The Sangha was not simply a collection of individuals following the Buddha independently. It was an organised community that maintained discipline and resolved disagreements.

According to the early Buddhist account, members discussed matters affecting the community and attempted to reach agreement through consensus. When agreement could not be achieved, decisions could be made through voting.

Meetings also helped settle disputes and address violations of monastic rules. This system gave the Sangha a collective role in preserving its standards of conduct.

The Buddhist Sangha was a religious monastic organisation. It should not be confused with political ganas or sanghas, such as the Vajji confederacy, which were forms of political organisation in ancient India.

Prelims focus

  • The Buddha established the Buddhist Sangha as an organised monastic community.
  • Bhikkhu means a Buddhist monk; bhikkhuni means a Buddhist nun.
  • The Vinaya Pitaka contains monastic rules and discipline.
  • A vihara is a Buddhist monastery.
  • The Sangha generally sought consensus and could use voting to resolve disagreements.
  • Trap: Lay supporters assisted the Sangha but were not automatically ordained members.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 7, 'New Questions and Ideas', printed pp. 70–72, 2018–19 edition; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', printed pp. 92–94; IGNOU, BHIC-101, Unit 12, 'Jainism, Buddhism and Ajivikas', section 'The Institution of Sangha', pp. 214–216.]

title: The Buddhist Sangha: Organisation, Membership and Daily Life

body:
Women and the early monastic order

In the beginning, the Buddhist monastic order admitted men. Women were subsequently permitted to renounce household life and join an organised community of Buddhist nuns.

The entry of women is associated with Mahaprajapati Gautami, also written Mahapajapati Gotami, and the intervention of the Buddha's disciple Ananda.

Mahaprajapati Gautami and the establishment of the nuns' order

Mahaprajapati Gautami was the Buddha's maternal aunt and foster mother. According to Buddhist tradition, she cared for Siddhartha Gautama after the death of his birth mother.

She wished to leave household life and enter the Buddhist monastic order. The accounts preserved in the Pali Vinaya describe her requesting permission for women to receive ordination.

The Buddha initially declined her requests. Mahaprajapati persisted, and other women also wished to enter the monastic community.

The role of Ananda

Ananda, an important disciple and attendant of the Buddha, intervened on behalf of Mahaprajapati Gautami and the other women.

According to the traditional account, Ananda asked whether women were capable of attaining the spiritual goals taught by the Buddha. The Buddha acknowledged that women possessed this capacity.

Ananda then referred to Mahaprajapati's role in raising the Buddha and again requested that women be allowed to enter the order.

The Buddha eventually permitted women's ordination. Mahaprajapati Gautami is traditionally recognised as the first Buddhist bhikkhuni.

Rules associated with women's ordination

The Pali Vinaya tradition records that Mahaprajapati accepted 8 special rules of respect, called garudhammas, in connection with her ordination.

These rules established additional obligations for the community of nuns. They included requirements concerning relations between monks and nuns, religious instruction and ordination procedures.

For example, the traditional rules required nuns to pay respect even to newly ordained monks, regardless of the nuns' seniority, and provided for the involvement of both the monks' and nuns' communities in the full ordination of women.

Thus, the Buddhist tradition recognised that women could attain spiritual liberation, while the institutional regulations for monks and nuns were not identical.

The account of Mahaprajapati's admission and the 8 garudhammas is preserved in Buddhist religious texts. It should be understood as a traditional account, rather than treating every detail of its transmission as an independently established historical event.

Women as teachers and members of the Sangha

Women who joined the Sangha followed a disciplined religious life. Like monks, they studied, meditated and participated in the transmission of Buddhist teachings.

Some became respected teachers. Early Buddhist literature uses the term theri for a respected senior nun, particularly one recognised for spiritual attainment.

The Therigatha, a collection of verses attributed to early Buddhist nuns, forms part of the Sutta Pitaka. It preserves accounts of women's religious experiences and their pursuit of liberation.

The participation of women was therefore not confined to receiving instruction. Buddhist nuns also contributed to the teaching and preservation of the religious tradition.

Distinguishing the important personalities

PersonConnection with the Sangha
Mahaprajapati GautamiThe Buddha's foster mother and the first woman traditionally recognised as a Buddhist nun.
AnandaThe Buddha's disciple who intervened to secure permission for women to enter the Sangha.

These roles should not be confused. Mahaprajapati Gautami sought admission and became the first bhikkhuni, whereas Ananda played the important mediating role.

Prelims focus

  • Mahaprajapati Gautami was the Buddha's foster mother.
  • She is traditionally regarded as the first Buddhist bhikkhuni.
  • Ananda persuaded the Buddha to permit women's entry into the Sangha.
  • The Pali Vinaya tradition associates women's ordination with 8 garudhammas.
  • The Therigatha contains verses attributed to Buddhist nuns and belongs to the Sutta Pitaka.
  • Trap: Ananda helped secure admission; he was not the first woman ordained.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', printed pp. 92–94; SuttaCentral, Anguttara Nikaya 8.51, 'Gotamisutta', translation by Bhikkhu Sujato, consulted 18 November 2026; Theravada Vinaya Pitaka, Bhikkhuni Khandhaka, Khandhaka 20, account of Mahapajapati Gotami, available through SuttaCentral, consulted 18 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The establishment of the nuns' order allowed women to pursue ordained Buddhist life.

title: Women's Entry into the Buddhist Sangha: Mahaprajapati Gautami and Ananda

body:
Meaning of the Tripitaka

The Buddha delivered his teachings orally. His disciples listened, memorised and repeated them. After his death, the preservation and transmission of these teachings became an important responsibility of the Buddhist community.

Over time, the teachings, disciplinary rules and systematic explanations were organised into collections of sacred literature.

Tripitaka is the Sanskrit name for the three principal collections or 'baskets' of Buddhist canonical literature. The corresponding Pali term is Tipitaka.

The 3 principal divisions are the Vinaya Pitaka, the Sutta Pitaka and the Abhidhamma Pitaka.

The Pali Tipitaka is the principal canonical collection preserved by the Theravada Buddhist tradition. Other Buddhist schools developed and transmitted related collections in different languages and forms. Therefore, the word Tripitaka describes a threefold canonical arrangement, not necessarily one identical set of texts followed by every Buddhist tradition.

Vinaya Pitaka: Rules and discipline

The Vinaya Pitaka contains regulations governing the conduct and organisation of Buddhist monks and nuns.

Its purpose was to maintain order within the Sangha and guide the behaviour of its members.

It deals with matters such as:

  • Rules of personal and communal conduct.
  • Admission and ordination into the monastic community.
  • Acceptable use of food, clothing and other necessities.
  • Procedures for dealing with violations of monastic discipline.
  • Organisation and functioning of the monastic community.

For example, Vinaya rules described limits on accepting food, obligations relating to shared accommodation and the proper treatment of communal possessions. Such provisions helped members maintain a simple and disciplined lifestyle.

The Patimokkha is the collection of fundamental monastic training rules recited within the Buddhist disciplinary tradition.

The Vinaya Pitaka is therefore the appropriate collection when a question concerns monastic rules, ordination or disciplinary procedures.

Sutta Pitaka: Discourses and teachings

The Sutta Pitaka contains discourses associated with the Buddha and his leading disciples. It presents teachings through sermons, explanations, conversations, stories and verses.

The Sanskrit equivalent of the Pali word sutta is sutra.

The Sutta Pitaka is the principal collection for studying the Buddha's teachings concerning suffering, ethical conduct, moderation, liberation and the practical application of the Dhamma.

The 5 Nikayas

In the Theravada Pali Canon, the Sutta Pitaka is organised into 5 Nikayas, or collections.

NikayaMain characteristic
Digha NikayaCollection of long discourses.
Majjhima NikayaCollection of middle-length discourses.
Samyutta NikayaDiscourses grouped by subject or connected themes.
Anguttara NikayaDiscourses arranged in numerical groups.
Khuddaka NikayaCollection of shorter and varied works, including verses and other texts.

Important examples

The Dhammapada, a collection of verses expressing Buddhist ethical and spiritual teachings, belongs to the Khuddaka Nikaya.

The Therigatha, containing verses attributed to early Buddhist nuns, also belongs to the Khuddaka Nikaya.

The Theragatha contains verses attributed to early Buddhist monks. It is another work within the same collection.

These examples show that the Sutta Pitaka is not limited to prose sermons. It also preserves religious teachings through poetry and other literary forms.

Abhidhamma Pitaka: Systematic analysis

The Abhidhamma Pitaka, corresponding to Abhidharma in Sanskrit, contains systematic and detailed explanations of Buddhist teachings.

Whereas the Sutta Pitaka commonly presents teachings through discourses and conversations, the Abhidhamma Pitaka examines their underlying concepts in a more analytical manner.

It gives particular attention to the classification and explanation of mental processes, experience and the principles used to understand reality within Buddhist philosophy.

The Pali Abhidhamma collection consists of 7 books. One of them is the Kathavatthu, traditionally associated with the monk Moggaliputta Tissa and the Third Buddhist Council.

The Abhidhamma literature developed through a process of systematisation over time. It should not be assumed that the complete later Abhidhamma Pitaka was already fixed in its surviving form immediately after the Buddha's death.

How the Buddhist canon was preserved

Early Buddhist teachings were transmitted through memorisation and collective recitation. Groups of monks preserved collections of teachings by repeatedly reciting them.

The Buddhist councils are traditionally connected with this process because they brought monks together to review teachings, discuss disciplinary questions and establish accepted interpretations.

According to Theravada tradition, the first council concentrated on the teachings and monastic discipline later associated with the Sutta and Vinaya collections. The Abhidhamma collection reached its developed form later.

The Pali canon was eventually written down in Sri Lanka, traditionally dated to the 1st century BCE. This was substantially later than the Buddha's lifetime.

Oral compilation and written recording are different events. Traditional accounts associate the First Buddhist Council with the recitation of teachings, not with the production of the complete surviving Pali Tripitaka as a written manuscript.

Distinguishing the 3 Pitakas

The clearest distinction is based on the type of content. The Vinaya concerns how the monastic community should conduct itself; the Sutta preserves religious discourses and teachings; and the Abhidhamma provides systematic analysis of those teachings.

For example, a rule about a monk's conduct belongs to the sphere of Vinaya. A discourse addressed to a householder belongs to the sphere of Sutta. A detailed classification of mental processes belongs to the sphere of Abhidhamma.

Prelims focus

  • Tripitaka is the Sanskrit term; Tipitaka is the Pali term.
  • Vinaya Pitaka: Rules and discipline of monks and nuns.
  • Sutta Pitaka: Discourses and teachings of the Buddha and his disciples.
  • Abhidhamma Pitaka: Systematic philosophical and psychological analysis.
  • The Sutta Pitaka contains 5 Nikayas.
  • The Dhammapada and Therigatha belong to the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Sutta Pitaka.
  • Trap: The entire surviving Tripitaka was not written down at the First Buddhist Council.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 4, 'Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings', printed pp. 91–94; Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, 'Pali Tipitaka Chanting: Oral Tradition of Theravada Buddhism', 2008, pp. 30–31; Daniel Veidlinger, 'History of the Buddhist Canon', Oxford Bibliographies in Buddhism, Introduction, published 13 September 2010, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: The Tripitaka: The Three Collections of Buddhist Sacred Literature
